notes: frater: genitive plural fratrum, not fraterum
pater: genitive plural patrum, not paterum
pastor: genitive plural pastorum
malleator: genitive plural malleatorum
custos: genitive plural custodum
soror: genitive plural sororum
livor: genitive plural livorum
sermo: genitive plural sermonum
ultio: genitive plural ultionum
iniquitas: genitive plural iniquitatum
civitas: genitive plural civitatum
sanguis: genitive plural sanguinum; the stem sanguin- shows only from the genitive on
grex: genitive plural gregum, and the stem greg- shows only from the genitive on
ovis: i-stem, genitive plural ovium
foris: i-stem, genitive plural forium; the singular is rare and the plural fores means one double door
adeps, adipis, c.: common gender, and the stem adip- shows only from the genitive on; genitive plural adipum
munus: genitive plural munerum, neuter plural munera
vulnus: genitive plural vulnerum, neuter plural vulnera
opus: genitive plural operum, neuter plural opera
æs, æris, n.: genitive plural ærum, neuter plural æra; the plural is rare in this sense
os, oris, n. (mouth) is a different word from os, ossis, n. (bone), and the two are identical in the nominative and accusative singular; genitive plural orum, neuter plural ora
faber, fabri, m.: the stem is fabr-, so there is no e after the nominative
ager, agri, m.: the stem is agr-, so there is no e after the nominative
agricola, agricolæ, m.: first declension but masculine, like nauta and poeta
appetitus, appetitus, m.: fourth declension, built on the supine stem of appeto
Ada, Adæ, f. and Sella, Sellæ, f. decline as first-declension nouns (Adæ, Sellæ in 4:23); Adæ is also the dative and genitive of Adam
Cain, Abel, Henoch, Irad, Maviaël, Mathusaël, Lamech, Jabel, Jubal, Tubalcain, Noëma, Seth, Enos and Eden are indeclinable; only the context gives their case
Henoch names two men — this son of Cain and the son of Jared in Genesis 5 — and Lamech likewise names this descendant of Cain and the father of Noë
Noëma occurs only here, in the nominative, so nothing shows whether it declines
major, majus is the comparative of magnus; superlative maximus
alter, altera, alterum: pronominal — genitive alterius, dative alteri
alius, alia, aliud: pronominal — genitive alterius, borrowed from alter, and dative alii
unus, una, unum: pronominal — genitive unius, dative uni
duo, duæ, duo: declines like nothing else in the language
septuplus, septupla, septuplum: the neuter septuplum stands as an adverb, 'sevenfold'
septuagies and septies are numeral adverbs and indeclinable
pario, parere, peperi, partus: the perfect peperi is reduplicated, and the present stem is pari- (paries, pariam)
gigno, gignere, genui, genitus: the present is reduplicated from the root gen-, which the perfect and supine show plain
cano, canere, cecini, cantus: the perfect cecini is reduplicated and weakens the a of the stem
cœpi, cœpisse: defective — perfect, pluperfect and future perfect only, with no present system at all
aio: defective — present indicative and a few subjunctive forms only, no perfect and no supine
concido, concidere, concidi: a compound of cado with no supine in use; the homograph concido, concidere, concidi, concisus (to cut to pieces) is a compound of cædo
concidit is both the present and the perfect third singular of concido; only the context separates them
occido, occidere, occidi, occisus (to kill) is a compound of cædo; the homograph occido, occidere, occidi, occasus (to fall, to set) is a compound of cado
offero, offerre, obtuli, oblatus: compound of fero, and the prefix assimilates twice over — of- before the f of fero, ob- before the t of tuli — so the perfect is obtuli, not oftuli
adsum, adesse, adfui: compound of sum; the perfect is also written affui
do, dare, dedi, datus: the only first-conjugation verb with a short stem vowel (das, dat, damus) and a reduplicated perfect dedi
fio, fieri, factus sum: passive in form, active in meaning, and its perfect is written as two words (factum est)
sum, esse, fui: no supine in use; adsum is its compound and inherits every form
possideo, possidere, possedi, possessus: the perfect possedi is shared with possido, possidere, possedi, possessus (to take possession of)
irascor, irasci, iratus sum: deponent with no supine of its own, and its perfect participle iratus is also used as a plain adjective, 'angry'
mereor, mereri, meritus sum: deponent, beside an active mereo of the same meaning
operor, operari, operatus sum: deponent, and operatus fueris in 4:12 is its future perfect written as two words
nascor, nasci, natus sum: deponent, and the supine stem nat- shares nothing with the present nasc-
egredior, egredi, egressus sum: deponent, and the supine stem egress- shares nothing with the present egred-
dominor, dominari, dominatus sum: deponent, and it governs the genitive here (dominaberis illius)
nescio, nescire, nescivi, nescitus: ne + scio, so the negative is inside the one word
maledico, maledicere, maledixi, maledictus: a compound of dico, so the imperative is maledic, not maledice
quam in 4:13 is the comparative particle 'than', not the accusative feminine of qui, quæ, quod — one surface form, two words
veniam in 4:13 is the accusative of venia (pardon), not the first singular of venio
egeris, invenerit and occiderit are future perfect indicative here; the same forms are also the perfect subjunctive
abscondar in 4:14 is the future passive; the same form is also the present passive subjunctive
cum is a conjunction here (cumque essent, cum operatus fueris) and a preposition elsewhere: one surface form, two words
habitantium and canentium are present participles used as nouns, so they take the genitive plural in -ium
